accuracy.evidence: Every number recomputed: 4 + 3 = 7 and 5 + 2 = 7 on fingers; 8 + 5 needs 13 > 10 fingers, ten frames show 10 + 3 = 13 (8 red then 5 blue, 2 blues complete the first frame); towers 9 − 6 = 3 with the extra 3 cubes highlighted; tool problems 2 + 3 = 5, 9 + 4 = 13, 7 vs 4; checks 7 − 3 = 4 (Sam said 5) and 10 − 4 = 6 (Ava said 7). Parameterised items enumerated by validate_lessons. Standards wording checked against EYFS ELG Number, NC England Y1 programme of study aims and CCSS K.OA.A.2.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets documented early-number slips: non-conservation of number (a longer spread-out row 'has more', Piaget; NCETM early number) in the step 3 predict, p3 and the 'longer' challenge tag; answering 'how many more' by adding (15 for 6 and 9; Fuson's comparison-problem research) in the tower buttons, m7 and tag 'add'; fingers seen as not allowed or enough for any sum (step 2 predict 'Yes, easily', tags fingers/hand/allowed); counting the full ten again instead of seeing 10 at a glance (ten-frame step, frame8/frame10 tags).

lab_distinct.evidence: gate_lab_distinct passed (under 30% similar to every flagship lab). 330 flagfing shows numbers on fingers and 561 flagrepnum builds numerals with counters, but neither asks the learner to choose between tools or to hit the 10-finger limit and switch to a ten frame. The fingers → ten frame hand-off, the spread-row vs tower comparison and the tool-for-the-job step are specific to selecting concrete tools, so the lab could not be relabelled for another topic.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner discovers each tool's job before it is stated: fingers work for 4 + 3, then visibly run out at 10 for 8 + 5 (the 11th tap is refused with 'Fingers ran out'), the ten frame then holds all 13 with a full ten visible; spread-out row A looks longer but its tower is shorter; the pick step asks for the tool and the feedback gives the reason (always with you / 10 at a glance / side by side). The last task uses counters to check a friend, so the tool becomes a way to verify, not only to answer.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting wrong options that the tasks disprove: 'Yes, easily' / 'Yes, on one hand' for 8 + 5 on fingers (disproved when the fingers run out), 'Row A, it is longer' for 6 spread out vs 9 bunched (disproved by the towers), and 'Fingers' for 9 + 4 (the pick step says 9 + 4 is more than 10). A.reveal reports the prediction in the done message.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions with tagged wrong answers, each with feedback naming the slip: fingers (10 fingers, 12 needed), hand (one hand has 5), pile vs full frame, longer (spread out is not more), same (one-to-one, 2 left over), frame8/frame10 (8 full so 2 empty), looks/allowed (pick a tool because it helps; fingers are fine but stop at 10), add (15 is adding, not 'how many more'), more (9 is Kim's total). Wrong taps in the lab also name the slip, e.g. 'Row A looked long, but its tower has only 6 cubes'.

readability.evidence: validate_lessons readability passed (kid under 6.5, adult under 9.5). Kid text uses short sentences and the precise early-maths terms ten frame, counters, cube towers, take away and how many more. Canvas text is one short instruction per step for ages 5–6; buttons say exactly what they do (Put up a finger, Add a red counter, Snap row A, Ava slipped: it is 6).

no_filler.evidence: gate_content found no filler phrases and explanation similarity under 12% to every lesson. Each kid paragraph carries one tool and what it is for (fingers to 10, ten frame for past 10, towers to compare and counters to check); the adult text gives the standards, the task order, the named slips and one teaching move (ask why that tool).

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 and 540 px screenshots for every step before and after Show me (/workspace/shots-0751/tools-ph-*, tools-p2-pre*, tools-d-*). After the first pass the finger height was raised, the finger count moved under the palms (it had overlapped the gap between hands), folded fingers drawn as short fingers, and row B packed into 55% of row A's length so the spread-out trick is visible on a phone. Tool tiles are about 110 px tall; ten-frame boxes about 34 px on a phone; every action also has a full-width button.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs passed on desktop and iPhone 13: all five tasks complete with Show me, challenge shown, axe WCAG 2.1 AA clean in both themes, no console errors. Every tap or drag has a button (Put up a finger, Put one down, Add a red/blue counter, Snap row A/B, Row B is taller, 3 more, tool names, Take one away, verdicts). The canvas aria-label states the fingers up, counters by colour, row/tower state or the problem after each action, and messages are spoken with c.say.
